column2: This coin isn't fair. It lands heads four times in five. Alice and Bob need it to settle a bet, and neither trusts what the other knows about it. They can still do it, perfectly fairly, using nothing but this coin.
The obvious way is to call it. One toss, heads or tails. But in a thousand tosses, heads comes up seven hundred ninety-one times. Whoever gets heads wins about four bets in five.
So a call is fair only if the caller has no idea which side the coin favours. And neither of them can check what the other knows.
An ordinary coin, tossed and caught, can't be weighted to do this. But a spun coin can be this unfair, and so can a loaded die.
So how could they make the bet fair, whatever either of them knows about the coin?
Toss the coin twice, and look at the two results as a pair.
A pair can be four things. Two heads, two tails, heads then tails, or tails then heads.
Picture every way the two tosses could go as a square. The first toss cuts it in two, with four fifths of the width for heads.
The second toss cuts it again, four fifths of the way up, at the same mark, because it's the same coin.
A block's share of the square is its pair's chance. Count the small squares. Two heads has sixteen of the twenty-five, and two tails has one. What about heads then tails, against tails then heads?
Four each. Exactly equal. Four in twenty-five is sixteen percent.
Alice calls heads then tails. Bob calls tails then heads. If the pair matches, throw it away and toss two fresh ones.
A thousand games with our coin. Alice wins four hundred ninety-four. Bob wins five hundred six.
The coin is as unfair as ever. The game isn't.
Why exactly equal? Heads then tails is four fifths wide and one fifth tall. Tails then heads is one fifth wide and four fifths tall.
Flip one across the diagonal and it lands on the other. The same two numbers, multiplied in the other order. And multiplying doesn't care about order.
Make the coin more unfair. Heads nine times in ten. Are the two blocks still equal?
Yes. Nine percent each. Slide the cuts anywhere, even past the middle so the coin favours tails. One block is always the mirror image of the other.
In letters, call the chance of heads p, so tails gets the rest, one minus p. Heads then tails is p times the rest. Tails then heads is the rest times p. Equal for every p.
So nobody needs to know how unfair the coin is, or which side it favours. And it makes no difference if one of them does know.
The trick does lean on two things. The coin's chance is the same on both tosses of a pair. And one toss doesn't affect the next, which is what independent means.
The trick has a price. With our coin, most pairs get thrown away. A pair decides only thirty-two times in a hundred.
So how many tosses does a game take, on average?
A pair decides about one time in three, so about three pairs. That's about six tosses. Exactly, six and a quarter.
Ten thousand games agree. They average six point two one tosses.
A fair coin still averages four tosses. A coin that lands heads ninety-nine times in a hundred averages about a hundred and one.
And nobody can promise when a game will stop. The longest of our ten thousand ran sixty tosses.
Now break it. Toss our unfair coin first, and a fair coin second. Is heads then tails still equal to tails then heads?
No. One cut moved and the other didn't, so the blocks aren't mirror images any more. Forty percent against ten. Alice wins four games in five, as if they'd never bothered.

A sneakier break is a coin with a memory. Count this one's heads and it looks fair, but it copies its last result four times in five. After two heads, heads then tails needs one change, and tails then heads needs two. So heads then tails is four times as likely, and after two tails it's the other way round.
The cure is to use only the tosses that come straight after a head. Each of those has the same chance, whatever came before it. So they behave like a plain unfair coin, and the trick handles that.
Back to why the trick works. Heads then tails and tails then heads hold the same results, one head and one tail, in a different order.
Try three tosses. Two tosses needed a square, so three need a cube.
Two heads then a tail. Heads, tails, heads. A tail then two heads. Which of these three patterns is likeliest?

None of them. Each is four fifths, times four fifths, times one fifth, in some order. The same slab, turned three ways. For tosses like ours, with the same chance every time and no memory, order never changes a chance.
So sort every pattern by its counts, how many heads and how many tails. Same counts, same chance. With two tosses the groups hold one, two and one, and the middle group is our trick.
Three tosses give one, three, three, one. Four tosses give one, four, six, four, one. You may know these numbers. It's Pascal's triangle.
The coin's unfairness only decides which group you land in. Inside a group, every pattern is equally likely. The counts carry the unfairness. The order is perfectly fair.
Look at the middle of the row for four tosses. Six patterns, all equally likely. What else has six equally likely results?
A die. Toss the coin four times. If exactly two are heads, the pattern picks the face. If not, toss four fresh ones.
Twenty-four thousand tosses of our unfair coin made nine hundred forty-nine rolls of a fair die. Each face came up about as often as a fair die's would.
It isn't cheap. A coin this unfair rarely gives exactly two heads in four. A roll costs about twenty-six tosses, on average.
There are cheaper rules built on the same idea. Any group of patterns with the same counts is a fair choice among them.
Now swap the coin for a loaded die. This one shows a six half the time.
Alice and Bob want to settle their bet with it. How would you do it?
Roll it twice. If the two rolls match, roll two fresh ones. If not, Alice wins when the first roll is bigger, and Bob wins when the second is.
It's the coin trick again. A six then a five is exactly as likely as a five then a six, and across the diagonal every block has an equal twin.
And a coin is just a die with two faces.
Three rolls do more, and three need the cube again, cut by the die's chances along every edge.
Say the rolls are a four, a five and a six, in some order. Each order lands in one of these six bricks. How do the bricks compare?
They're one brick, turned six ways. A tenth, by a fifth, by a half. The same three rolls have the same chance in any order.
So when three rolls all differ, the order they came in is a fair choice among six. Low, high, middle is one order. High, low, middle is another. If any two match, roll three fresh ones.
Six thousand rolls of the loaded die made six hundred fifty rolls of a fair one.
It keeps going, up to six rolls. Four different rolls can come in twenty-four orders. But rolls that all differ get rarer, so each step costs more.

The trick comes from the mathematician John von Neumann, in a talk in nineteen forty-nine. The printed summary calls it rigorously unbiased, which is to say exactly fair. It also names the price. At most twenty-five percent as efficient as ordinary coin tossing.
Our coin gives less. A hundred tosses give about sixteen fair ones. Could a better rule get all hundred?

No. Guess heads and you're right four times in five, so each toss of this coin holds less than a fair one. The most any rule can average is just over seventy-two. That ceiling is called the coin's entropy.

You get closer by wasting less. Use the bigger groups in deeper rows of the triangle, or run the trick again and again on the two things it ignored. Both climb toward the ceiling, and however far you go, they stop just short of it.
Computers need fair tosses too, for passwords and secret codes. Many get them from electrical noise, and raw noise comes out a little unfair. What would you do with it?
Pair the readings up, and throw away the pairs that match. In nineteen ninety-nine, one chip maker, Intel, built a corrector based on this trick into its random number generator.
So an unfair coin like ours still has a fair one inside it, as long as it can land both ways. You find it by setting aside how many heads came up, and looking only at the order.
